key_findings.value: Deformation substructure consists of straight, near-screw-oriented superdislocations (2 (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials) plus numerous edge dislocation dipoles and loops (Fig. 14); stepped structures and dislocation pairs from reactions (Fig. 15); reaction-produced dislocation pairs together with APBII residual-contrast fringes traversing the area (Fig. 16).

unmapped_findings: Fe–30% Al is described as a weakly DO3-ordered material that deforms by the movement of superdislocations composed of two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials (perfect superdislocations of the B2 lattice).

For Fe–30% Al the APBI fault energy is sufficiently high that the separation of the partials constituting the superdislocation is small; the parallel image pairs visible in Fig. 14 (right) all correspond to short or long dipole dislocation pairs rather than separated partials.

Dislocation pairs observed in deformed Fe–30% Al (Figs. 15 and 16) are the result of dislocation reactions and do not correspond to the partials of the glissile superdislocations; reactions lead to stepped structures.

Fringes traversing the deformed Fe–30% Al areas (Fig. 16) are residual APBII contrast, produced because the pairs of (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials destroy some of the DO3 order during movement in this weakly DO3-ordered material.

In situ straining of a Fe–30% Al alloy (Ref. [32], cited in b0056) showed spontaneous formation of dipole debris behind moving screw dislocations without apparent intersection with any forest dislocation or other debris.

The work hardening rate of Fe–Al alloys shows a sharp maximum near Fe–28% Al, coinciding with an equally strong maximum in elastic anisotropy; this is attributed to strong Peierls forces for compositions close to 25–30% Al rather than to elastic anisotropy itself.
